Unless one index holds all of them, each row found through an index costs a key lookup into the table, and past a few thousand rows the optimizer drops the index and scans the whole table. Wide rows also inflate the memory reserved for sorts. Name the columns the caller uses, and cover the hot queries with included columns.
An admin screen lists the last 30 days of orders: date, status and total. There's an index on

. In a test on SQL Server 2022 with 1,000,000 orders, it ignored that index, scanned all 50,391 pages of the table, and reserved 267 MB of memory to sort 41,096 rows. Asking for the four columns the screen shows, with those columns in the index, read 196 pages and needed no sort at all. Over three runs each, that was about 309 ms against 23 ms on average.

It's half true, which is why it survives. Fetching one order by its primary key is a single clustered index seek, and the whole row is right there, so the extra columns really do cost only bytes. ORMs load whole entities by default, and on a development database with a few hundred rows nothing is ever slow. The bytes are real, too: in the test, the 30-day result carried about 9 MB of column data against about 1 MB for the four columns. But the bytes were the smallest part of the bill.
A nonclustered index holds a few columns and a pointer

In SQL Server, a nonclustered index row holds its key columns, any included columns, and a row locator: the clustered index key, or a row ID when the table is a heap. Any other column has to come from the table itself, through a
: one more seek down the clustered index for every row the index found. In the test, a customer's 52 orders read 171 pages with
, columns the page never showed. With the needed columns in the index, the same query read 3 pages.

PostgreSQL works the same way with different names. Every index is stored apart from the table's heap, so an ordinary index scan visits the heap for each row. When the index holds every column the query references, the planner can use an index-only scan instead.
Past a point, the optimizer drops your index
Lookups are random reads, one per row, so the optimizer weighs them against reading the whole table in order. In the test,

The index never changed. What changed is how many rows needed the other columns, and at 30 days the whole table was cheaper. A
has no such limit, because there is nothing to look up.
Wide rows make sorts reserve more memory
Before a sort or hash runs, SQL Server reserves memory for it, a
, sized from the estimated row count and row width. The

, and the plan estimated the average row at 4,574 bytes, while the real rows held about 230 bytes of data. The first run was granted 267 MB and used 21 MB. Row mode memory grant feedback, on at compatibility level 150 and above, cut later runs to 164 MB, still nearly eight times what was used. Microsoft's page on the feature puts it plainly: excessive grants result in wasted memory and reduced concurrency.

Name the columns, then cover them

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
-- Admin list: the screen shows CreatedAt, Status and Total
SELECT *
FROM dbo.Orders
WHERE CreatedAt >= '2026-10-02'
ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC;
-- Tested: Clustered Index Scan + Sort, 50,391 reads,
-- 267 MB memory grant on the first run

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
-- Key: what the query filters and sorts on; INCLUDE: what it returns
CREATE INDEX IX_Orders_CreatedAt
    ON dbo.Orders (CreatedAt)
    INCLUDE (Status, Total)
    WITH (DROP_EXISTING = ON);

SELECT Id, CreatedAt, Status, Total
FROM dbo.Orders
WHERE CreatedAt >= '2026-10-02'
ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC;
-- Tested: Index Seek, 196 reads, no Sort, no memory grant

syntax and wasn't run for this article. If an ORM writes your SQL, the same rule applies: a query that loads whole entities selects every mapped column, while a projection into a DTO selects only the ones it names. The .NET path's article "Beyond Include: Fixing N+1 in EF Core With Projections and Split Queries" covers that side.
Every included column is a second copy, written on every insert and on every update that changes it. In the test, adding

grew the two indexes from 2,526 and 2,026 pages to 5,217 and 4,722. Microsoft's design guide warns against covering indexes with too many columns, and PostgreSQL adds a catch of its own: an index-only scan still visits the heap for any page not marked all-visible in the visibility map, so on a table that changes quickly, included columns may buy little.

blocks.title: Let the plan write the INCLUDE list

content.text: In SQL Server, open the Key Lookup operator and read its Output List: those are exactly the columns the index is missing. In the test, it listed

How to apply it in your project

Look for Key Lookup operators in the plans of your most frequent and most expensive queries, or for index scans that aren't index-only in PostgreSQL. Check the row counts: a lookup per row adds up fast.
and whole-entity loads with the columns the caller actually uses. On its own this shrinks rows and memory grants, and it makes covering possible.

. Only do it for queries that run often or read a lot, not for every list in the app.
Compare index size and write timings before and after, and confirm with the actual plan that the lookup is gone.

items.text: costs reads, not just bytes: every column outside the index means a key lookup per row.
Past a few thousand rows, the optimizer may skip your index for a full scan: 50,391 reads instead of 196 in the test.
Wide columns inflate memory grants: 267 MB reserved, 21 MB used for one sort in the test.
A covering index answers from the index alone; in PostgreSQL that's an index-only scan, which also depends on the visibility map.
Included columns are copies, so cover the hot queries only and measure the write cost.
